title: Scaling with parallelism
hypothesis: Doubling the cores available to Spark gives at least 1.6 times speed-up.
conclusion: local[1]: 28.3s wall clock, 27.8s of work after removing 0.5s of fixed cost; local[2]: 22.6s wall clock, 22.1s of work after removing 0.5s of fixed cost; local[4]: 21.2s wall clock, 20.9s of work after removing 0.3s of fixed cost. Speed-up on the work component against one core: local[1] 1.0x, local[2] 1.258x, local[4] 1.33x. Doubling from 2 to 4 cores gave 1.057x, against the hypothesis's 1.6x threshold: not met.. Core utilisation (executor run time over wall clock x cores): local[1] 0.731, local[2] 0.721, local[4] 0.67; shuffle written: local[1] 21321424 bytes, local[2] 23754093 bytes, local[4] 24268426 bytes; spill: local[1] 0 bytes, local[2] 0 bytes, local[4] 0 bytes. Sub-linear scaling is the expected observation; the window aggregations shuffle, and shuffling does not halve when the cores double. This is intra-node scaling inside one JVM, not distributed workers, and the 100 GB tier was not run - see the limitations.
limitations: The 100 GB tier was not run and is not estimated: Docker has a 5.27 GB VM here (ADR-0002).

Distributed workers were not used. Compose can start a Spark master and one worker, but with 8 logical cores and ~3 GB usable for containers two workers would contend for the same cores and the result would measure scheduling overhead, not scaling. `local[N]` varies the same knob - cores available to the work - inside one JVM, so there is no network shuffle and no cross-machine spill. The numbers below describe intra-node scaling only.

The host is an AMD Ryzen 5 2500U, 4 cores and 8 threads: the Docker VM's 8 vCPUs are 4 physical cores with two hardware threads each. local[4] therefore runs four threads that share physical cores with each other and with every other process in the VM, so going from 2 to 4 is not a doubling of compute, and the 2-to-4 ratio below is a lower bound on what doubling real cores would give.
